findings.claim: FlexPrefill's sparse pattern determination and Vertical-Slash index selection rely on the last block_size query vectors as a representative query set; this can fail when earlier queries have different attention patterns.
findings.mechanism: The method estimates attention distributions and vertical/slash line importance from only Q[-block_size:], then extends those estimates to all queries. If earlier queries attend differently, the selected sparse indices can be inaccurate.
conditions: Attention patterns vary across query positions

evidence.location: Section 3, Query-Aware Sparse Pattern Determination, step 1 Representative Query Selection
evidence.support_description: Selects the last block_size query vectors as the representative subset.
Replacing the representative query subset for Vertical-Slash index selection with the middle block drops average RULER score from 89.18 to 38.18.

caveats: Ablation is only on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and RULER.
Replacing the subset for pattern determination had little effect; sensitivity is mainly for Vertical-Slash index selection.

findings.claim: FlexPrefill requires model/task-specific tuning of the JSD threshold tau and cumulative-attention threshold gamma; poor settings can misclassify heads or over-sparsify attention and degrade performance.
findings.mechanism: Tau controls whether a head is treated as Query-Aware or Vertical-Slash, while gamma controls how much attention mass is retained. Fixed defaults may not suit all models or tasks; too-large tau admits inaccurate Query-Aware heads, and too-low gamma drops important tokens.
conditions: Default tau=0.1 and gamma=0.9/0.95 used in experiments

evidence.support_description: Tau is set to 0.1 for all models; gamma is set to 0.9 for Yi/Qwen and 0.95 for other models.
An appropriate tau improves performance, but too-large tau can classify inaccurate heads as Query-Aware and degrade performance.
Lowering gamma speeds up inference but reduces average RULER score, e.g., LLaMA gamma=0.95 avg 89.18 vs gamma=0.6 avg 83.25.
Optimal tau varies by model; GLM is best at tau=0.2, Qwen at tau=0.1, etc.

caveats: The paper provides empirical defaults and shows a speed-performance trade-off.
Sensitivity magnitude varies by model and benchmark.

findings.claim: FlexPrefill needs a minimum computational budget, such as at least 1024 tokens and first/last key blocks, to prevent attention-head collapse under high sparsity; without it, low gamma can cause malfunction.
findings.mechanism: Cumulative-attention selection can choose too few tokens for some heads when gamma is low, causing sparse attention to miss necessary context. The paper adds a heuristic floor to avoid this collapse.
conditions: Some attention heads select insufficient tokens

evidence.support_description: Retains the first and last key blocks of each query block and requires each attention head to compute at least 1024 tokens.

evidence.location: Section 4.3 Minimum Budget Limit; Appendix F.5, Table 10
evidence.support_description: With smaller gamma, some heads may be insufficient; a minimum budget significantly enhances performance and prevents collapse.

caveats: When gamma is high, the minimum budget is unnecessary.
Increasing the minimum budget beyond a point does not improve results.

findings.claim: Imposing a maximum computational budget can degrade performance for some models, especially LLaMA at long contexts, so a universal cap is not safe.
findings.mechanism: Capping per-head computation limits the number of selected tokens. If important attention mass lies beyond the cap, accuracy drops, and the effect is model-specific.
conditions: Models with broad attention needs such as LLaMA

evidence.support_description: LLaMA 128k score drops from 79.09 without cap to 75.72 with 32k cap, 72.12 with 16k cap, and 65.87 with 8k cap; GLM can maintain or improve.

caveats: Only RULER results are shown.
Some models benefit from maximum budget caps.

findings.claim: FlexPrefill accelerates only the pre-filling phase; it does not provide sparse attention for decoding, and experiments switch to dense computation during decoding.
findings.mechanism: The method dynamically selects sparse indices for prompt prefill. Decoding uses dense attention in the evaluation, so end-to-end generation speedup is limited to the prefill stage.

evidence.support_description: Focuses on long-sequence inference, especially the attention pre-filling phase.
All baselines use sparse computation during pre-filling and switch to dense computation during the decoding stage.

caveats: The paper's scope is prefill; it does not claim to be a decoding method.
Decoding acceleration may be addressed by other methods.

findings.claim: The method is validated only on four LLMs, two long-context benchmarks, a single A100 GPU, block_size=128, and greedy decoding; generalization to other architectures, tasks, hardware, and sampling strategies is not established.
findings.mechanism: Sparse pattern prevalence and optimal thresholds may differ across models and tasks, and implementation details are hardware-dependent. The evidence base cannot guarantee performance outside the tested settings.

evidence.support_description: Uses four models, RULER and InfiniteBench, a single A100 80GB GPU, block_size=128, and greedy decoding.

caveats: Limited scope is common in research and is not proof of failure.
Appendix F.2 shows block size 64 vs 128 had little effect on tested models.

findings.claim: The Query-Aware vs Vertical-Slash decision uses a heuristic JSD threshold on block-pooled attention distributions estimated from a representative query subset; there is no formal guarantee that this classification minimizes attention error.
findings.mechanism: The method compares average-pooled estimated attention with sum-pooled true attention via sqrt(JSD) and compares the result to tau. The choice of tau and pooling is empirical, and the relationship between JSD and final sparse-attention error is not theoretically established.

evidence.location: Section 3, Query-Aware Sparse Pattern Determination, steps 2-4; Algorithm 2
evidence.support_description: Computes block-pooled distributions and compares sqrt(JSD) to a predefined tau.
Ablation shows tau choice affects performance; too-large tau can misclassify heads.

caveats: JSD is motivated by symmetry and boundedness.
The paper empirically validates tau on tested models.

findings.claim: The cumulative-attention threshold gamma optimizes selected attention mass, but the theoretical error bound depends on value vectors and is not tight; high attention mass does not always guarantee minimal output difference.
findings.mechanism: Equation 3 selects the smallest index set whose normalized attention scores exceed gamma. Appendix A bounds output error by (1-a_S) sum |v_j|, which depends on values and is an upper bound. Minimizing set size subject to attention mass is a proxy, not direct minimization of attention output error.

evidence.location: Section 3, Cumulative-Attention Based Index Selection, Equation 3
evidence.support_description: Selects indices until cumulative normalized attention score exceeds gamma.
The error upper bound includes sum of |v_j| and (1-a_S), showing dependence on values and a loose bound.

caveats: The proxy is theoretically motivated and empirically effective.
The bound may be loose but useful.

findings.claim: When JSD is at least tau, FlexPrefill falls back to a conservative Vertical-Slash pattern, which may miss query-specific diverse attention patterns and reduce accuracy for heads with non-structured sparsity.
findings.mechanism: The fallback uses a structured vertical/slash index set extended from representative queries. If the head actually has diverse query-specific blocks, those blocks may not be selected.
conditions: Head has diverse or query-specific attention

evidence.support_description: If DJS >= tau, the method falls back to the Vertical-Slash pattern using a subset of queries and extends it globally.
Most attention heads use Vertical-Slash patterns, with fewer Query-Aware patterns mainly in the first layer.

caveats: The fallback is intended to be conservative when estimation is unreliable.
The paper shows overall performance is preserved on tested benchmarks.

findings.claim: Query-Aware index selection flattens and normalizes the estimated attention map globally, selecting a single global set of blocks rather than per-query blocks; this can over- or under-allocate computation across queries.
findings.mechanism: Algorithm 4 flattens the pooled attention map and selects top blocks until global cumulative mass exceeds gamma. This ignores per-query budget differences; a block important for one query may consume budget while another query's needs are unmet.

evidence.location: Section 3, Query-Aware head index selection; Algorithm 4
evidence.support_description: Flattens and normalizes the attention map, sorts it, and selects until the global sum exceeds gamma.
An alternative per-query implementation achieves comparable performance; global flatten is chosen for implementation efficiency.

caveats: The alternative per-query implementation had comparable performance in tested models.
The global approach may be efficient and adequate.

findings.claim: FlexPrefill operates at block granularity, with block_size=128, for estimation and selection, so it may not capture fine-grained token-level sparse patterns within blocks.
findings.mechanism: Pooling and block-wise attention estimation aggregate tokens into blocks. Selected blocks are computed densely, so intra-block sparsity is not exploited and coarse blocks may include irrelevant tokens.

evidence.location: Section 3, Block-Wise Attention Estimation; Section 4.1 Implementation Details
evidence.support_description: Uses pooling with kernel size block_size and block_size=128 in all experiments.
Block size 64 vs 128 did not significantly affect performance on tested models.

caveats: Block size ablation showed little effect on tested models.
Block granularity is common for GPU efficiency.

findings.claim: FlexPrefill introduces pattern-search and index-construction overhead; at shorter input lengths non-attention overhead is higher, so benefits are mainly for long sequences.
findings.mechanism: The method adds representative attention computation, JSD pattern search, and O(n log n) index construction. These costs are relatively large for short sequences where dense attention is already cheap.

evidence.support_description: At shorter input lengths, non-attention computation overheads are higher; as input length increases, index search percentage decreases.

caveats: The paper targets long-sequence inference; short-sequence overhead may be acceptable.
Overhead is offset at long lengths.

findings.claim: FlexPrefill does not always preserve full-attention performance; on some models and tasks, average or task scores can be lower than full attention.
findings.mechanism: Sparse approximation can miss relevant tokens for certain retrieval, QA, or math tasks, causing accuracy degradation despite speedup.

evidence.support_description: Yi average: Full-attn 37.69 vs Ours 36.18; other task-level results also vary, showing mixed preservation.

caveats: Many tasks are preserved or improved; differences can be small.
Table 2 shows mixed results, not uniform degradation.

findings.claim: FlexPosit's main quantization scheme is weight-only; activations remain FP16, so it does not by itself deliver low-bit activation inference.
findings.mechanism: Only weights are quantized with channel-wise Posit; activations stay FP16 in the main evaluation, with FP8 activation quantization only as a supplementary experiment.
conditions: Workloads where activation memory or activation compute dominates

evidence.support_description: States that only weights are quantized while activations remain in FP16.
FP8 activation quantization is reported as a supplementary setting, not the main method.

caveats: The paper shows FP8 activation quantization is largely orthogonal and preserves relative ordering.

findings.claim: Fractional precision is a statistical average over channel windows, not continuous per-weight or per-channel precision.
findings.mechanism: The GPCU runs each channel window at an integer bit-serial depth P; virtual precision bvirt is obtained by mixing discrete 4/5-bit windows.
conditions: Need for true per-weight fractional precision
Fine-grained mixed precision within a channel window

evidence.support_description: Describes weighted combination of discrete bit-widths at channel-window granularity.
Defines bvirt as a fractional mean bit-width from upgrading channel windows.
GPCU defines a P-cycle precision window per GEMM kernel.

caveats: This design preserves systolic regularity and is the intended hardware knob.

findings.claim: Precision granularity is tied to systolic-array-aligned channel windows, so all weights in a window share one precision and simultaneous mixed precision within a tile is not supported.
findings.mechanism: Channel windows are integer multiples of array columns; GPCU globally synchronizes PEs to one precision window; precision changes only at channel-window boundaries.

evidence.support_description: All weights in a channel window share the same precision within 4-8 bits.
Precision changes occur only at channel-window boundaries and GPCU synchronizes all PEs.

caveats: The paper argues this is necessary for regular systolic dataflow.

findings.claim: Sensitivity profiling is expensive because it re-evaluates full-model perplexity for each channel window.
findings.mechanism: Algorithm 2 quantizes the model, then upgrades one channel window at a time and recomputes PPL for every window.
conditions: Large models with many channel windows

evidence.support_description: Loops over all channel windows and evaluates PPL for each upgrade.
Describes profiling one channel window at a time while the rest remain at baseline.

caveats: Profiling is offline; Fisher-ranked allocation is presented as a lower-cost proxy but is less effective.

findings.claim: The sensitivity-guided allocation is greedy and ignores interactions among channel windows.
findings.mechanism: Each window's ΔPPL is measured with only that window upgraded from baseline; allocation then upgrades top-ranked windows until the mean precision budget is met.

evidence.support_description: Measures ΔPPL for one window at a time with the rest at baseline.
Allocation upgrades most sensitive windows until weighted mean precision reaches bvirt.

caveats: The paper shows this ranking outperforms random, location, and Fisher-ranked allocation in their experiments.

findings.claim: The Posit exponent size is fixed to es=1 and the per-channel scale is restricted to a power of two with a 4-bit index, limiting scale resolution and range.
findings.mechanism: es=1 is adopted as a fixed setting for the low-bit regime; Algorithm 1 selects among candidate power-of-two scales by SQNR; a 4-bit index stores the scale.
conditions: Models or precisions where another es would be better
Channels needing finer-than-power-of-two scaling or a wider scale range

evidence.support_description: States es=1 is fixed for the evaluated low-bit regime and a 4-bit index stores the per-channel scale.
Sweeps candidate power-of-two scales and selects by SQNR.

caveats: Power-of-two scaling avoids FP multipliers and keeps metadata small; es=1 was strongest among evaluated 4-bit Posit configurations.

findings.claim: The architecture supports 4-8 bits, but the evaluation only covers roughly 4-5 bits; sub-4-bit and 6-8-bit behavior are not demonstrated.
findings.mechanism: The bit-serial datapath supports P from 4 to 8, but experiments sweep virtual precision from 4 to 5 bits and report sub-5-bit weights.

evidence.support_description: Claims tunable fractional precision from 4 to 8 bits.
Precision sweep is 4-5 bits with 0.1-bit steps.
Reported FlexPosit results are 4.1-5.0 bits.

caveats: The paper targets sub-5-bit edge inference, so 6-8-bit evaluation may be outside its main scope.

findings.claim: Accuracy is not uniformly near-FP16; at 4.1 bits the mean ΔPPL is 0.64, and matching BitMoD can require up to 5.0 bits for some models.
findings.mechanism: Channel-wise Posit plus mixed-precision allocation reduces but does not eliminate the accuracy gap; larger/heavy-tailed models need more precision.

evidence.support_description: FlexPosit at 4.1 b has mean ΔPPL 0.64; PEB requires up to 5.0 b for Qwen2.5-14B.
Downstream MMLU/HellaSwag accuracy at 5.0 b remains below FP16 for several models.

caveats: At PEB the mean ΔPPL is 0.33, and Best-PPL reaches 0.20; the paper describes this as near-FP16, not exact.

findings.claim: Hardware results are based on RTL simulation, synthesis, and cycle-level modeling rather than a fabricated chip.
findings.mechanism: Verilog RTL simulation, Synopsys 16 nm synthesis, cycle-level simulator, Ramulator DDR4, and CACTI buffer models are used.

evidence.support_description: Describes Verilog RTL simulation, 16 nm synthesis, cycle-level simulator, Ramulator, and CACTI.

caveats: This is standard pre-silicon methodology; the paper does not claim measured silicon.

findings.claim: The design relies on channel-wise quantization regularity and per-column rescaling; it does not natively support group-wise or irregular outlier-aware layouts.
findings.mechanism: Output-stationary systolic array uses per-column rescale units; group-wise quantization would require per-PE rescale and irregular alignment.

evidence.support_description: Contrasts per-group misalignment with per-channel column-aligned streams.
Group-wise requires per-PE rescale; channel-wise uses per-column rescale.
Per-group FlexPosit variant increases rescale area overhead from 0.4% to 9.4%.

caveats: The paper argues channel-wise regularity is the key efficiency advantage; a per-group variant is possible but costs more.

findings.claim: SerialPosit uses sign-magnitude encoding and Posits only for weight storage, so it loses encoded-domain operations such as direct comparison and negation and does not provide Posit-domain compute.
findings.mechanism: Sign-magnitude encoding enables bit-serial decoding; weights are decoded to FP before arithmetic; Posit is not used for intermediate computation.

evidence.support_description: States SerialPosit loses encoded-domain operations such as direct comparison and negation, and Posits are used only for weight storage.
Shows sign-magnitude SerialPosit versus conventional two's-complement Posit.

caveats: The lost operations are unnecessary for the paper's weight-only storage use case.

findings.claim: Throughput decreases as precision increases because the bit-serial depth P grows; the 4-way cluster only restores full rate at the minimum 4-bit precision.
findings.mechanism: Each cluster achieves 4/P MACs per cycle for 4≤P≤8; latency increases nearly linearly with precision.

evidence.support_description: States effective throughput is 4/P MACs per cycle and matches FP16 MAC at 4 b.
Shows normalized latency increasing nearly linearly with precision.

caveats: This is the intended accuracy-throughput trade-off; FlexPosit still wins under iso-area iso-PPL comparisons.

findings.claim: Evaluation is limited to edge-scale models up to 14B and a small benchmark set, so generality to larger models, MoE, long-context, and broader tasks is not established.
findings.mechanism: Models include GPT-2, Phi-2, OPT-2.7B, LLaMA-2-7B, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-7B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B; PPL on WikiText-2 and MMLU/HellaSwag.
conditions: Long-context or generative tasks beyond evaluated benchmarks

evidence.support_description: Lists evaluated models and WikiText-2 protocol.
Downstream evaluation is limited to MMLU and HellaSwag.

caveats: The paper explicitly targets edge-scale LLMs; the selected models are representative of that scope.

findings.claim: The main datapath uses FP16 activations and FP16 accumulation, so benefits depend on FP16 support and it is not an integer-only low-bit accelerator.
findings.mechanism: MAC clusters process FP16 activations and share an FP16 accumulator; weights are decoded to FP-domain terms.

evidence.support_description: Activations remain FP16 in the main method.
PEs operate on FP16 activations and share an FP16 accumulator.

caveats: Table VI shows FP8 activation quantization is largely orthogonal, but it is not the main configuration.

findings.claim: Precision allocation is static and offline per model/calibration set; there is no runtime input-adaptive precision control.
findings.mechanism: Sensitivity profiling and allocation are precomputed; GPCU receives the target precision schedule for each GEMM kernel/channel window.

evidence.support_description: Profiling uses a dataset D and precomputes ranked sensitivities.
GPCU receives target precision P determined by channel-window-level precision adaptation.

caveats: Offline MPQ is common and reduces runtime overhead; the paper does not claim runtime adaptivity.

findings.claim: QoServe's QoS model distinguishes only interactive and non-interactive classes; custom SLO targets within a class do not provide arbitrary fine-grained QoS classes.
findings.mechanism: Deadline and scheduling logic is specialized for interactive TTFT/TBT and non-interactive TTLT; there is no general N-class deadline model.
conditions: Workloads require more than two semantic QoS classes
Applications need mixed or additional latency metrics beyond TTFT/TBT/TTLT
caveats: Application owners can set custom SLO values within each class
The paper evaluates three buckets by splitting non-interactive into two SLO tiers

evidence.support_description: Defines two QoS classes: interactive and non-interactive; custom SLO targets are within the class.

findings.claim: Empirical validation is limited to three models, two GPU types, three traces, and Poisson arrivals; generality to other models, hardware, traces, and arrival processes is not established.
findings.mechanism: Evaluation setup uses Llama3-8B, Qwen-7B, Llama3-70B on A100/H100 with ShareGPT and Azure traces; arrivals generated as Poisson.
conditions: Deploying on other model families or sizes
Using non-Poisson or bursty production arrival patterns
Using other hardware or parallelism configurations
caveats: The authors include multiple models, TP degrees, and hardware platforms to show diversity
Artifact supports some reproduction

evidence.support_description: Models/hardware and datasets listed; request arrival times generated using Poisson distribution.

findings.claim: Dynamic chunking depends on a random-forest latency predictor trained per model, hardware, and parallelism; prediction error and deliberate under-prediction can limit chunk-size optimality.
findings.mechanism: Predictor estimates batch execution time from profiles; it is tuned to under-predict chunk size to avoid latency increases.
caveats: Prediction runs on CPU with negligible overhead
Under-prediction is claimed to scarcely miss throughput maximization

evidence.support_description: Random forest predicts batch execution time; trained on Vidur profiles for each model, hardware, and parallelism; <10% error; tuned to under-predict.

findings.claim: For non-interactive requests, priority calculation needs decode length, which is unknown; QoServe approximates it from per-application history using two standard deviations, so priority can be inaccurate for new or heavy-tailed applications.
findings.mechanism: Eq. 5 includes remaining decode time; history-based over-approximation by two standard deviations is used because decode length is unknown.

Non-interactive requests with highly variable output lengths
caveats: Paper reports the simple prediction sufficiently captures priority in its evaluation

findings.claim: Hybrid prioritization depends on the alpha hyperparameter, which is tuned offline for fixed QPS and load-adaptively for variable QPS; performance and fairness may vary with workload and load.
findings.mechanism: Priority is a linear combination of EDF deadline and SRPF remaining work; alpha controls how strongly long requests are deprioritized.

caveats: Paper provides tuning guidance: alpha=8 ms/token for fixed QPS, alpha=1 ms/token at low load for variable QPS
Figure 14 shows trade-off

evidence.support_description: Alpha configurable; offline sweep 0-10; 8 ms/token best fixed-QPS; variable-QPS uses load-adaptive tuning; Figure 14 shows median latency and violations vary with alpha.

findings.claim: Eager relegation can delay relegated requests substantially and provides no hard completion-time bound; under sustained overload the relegated queue may grow if there are insufficient low-load periods.
findings.mechanism: Requests about to violate are moved to a relegated queue and serviced opportunistically during lower load.
caveats: Paper demonstrates eventual completion and graceful degradation in transient overload
In transient overload, all important requests met SLOs and 8.64% overall violations

evidence.support_description: Relegated requests serviced opportunistically during lower load; max latency for relegated requests observed up to 3900s in transient overload.

findings.claim: QoServe never preempts requests in the decode queue, so a newly arriving higher-priority request may wait behind ongoing decode work.
findings.mechanism: Selective preemption only preempts in-flight prefill requests; decode requests are protected to avoid TBT violations and KV-cache overhead.
conditions: Strict TBT decode requests occupy the batch
Need to preempt decode work to meet a tighter deadline
caveats: Design protects TBT and reduces memory pressure

evidence.support_description: Preempt only if in-flight request is in prefill queue; requests in decode queue are never preempted.

findings.mechanism: Decode replicas are not differentiated by TBT SLO in the disaggregated evaluation.

evidence.support_description: Quest retains all of the KV cache and selects part of the KV cache based on the current query.
Quest reduces memory movement from the entire KV cache to metadata and constant K pages, not total KV cache size.

caveats: Quest is compatible with existing quantization mechanisms.
The method targets latency reduction rather than memory capacity reduction.

findings.claim: Quest's criticality estimation adds metadata-loading overhead that can underutilize GPU memory bandwidth at short sequence lengths, limiting speedup for shorter contexts.
findings.mechanism: Quest loads min/max vectors for every page during criticality estimation; at short sequence lengths the total memory load is insufficient to saturate GPU bandwidth, so relative latency is worse than FlashInfer.

evidence.support_description: At short sequence length, criticality estimation memory bandwidth utilization is smaller than FlashInfer; relative performance improves as sequence length grows.

caveats: At long sequence lengths, relative criticality estimation latency approaches 1/Page Size.
Quantization or larger page size can further reduce additional memory usage.

findings.claim: Quest incurs Top-K filtering overhead and requires dedicated CUDA/FlashInfer/PageAttention implementation, which may limit portability and add a small fixed cost.
findings.mechanism: Quest uses a batched Top-K CUDA operator from RAFT and dedicated CUDA kernels based on FlashInfer; Top-K filtering has a small latency overhead.

evidence.support_description: Top-K filtering has a low latency overhead of 5-10 us for sequence length less than 128k.
The framework is implemented with dedicated CUDA kernels based on FlashInfer.
The Top-K operator overhead is not included in the efficiency analysis.

caveats: The Top-K overhead is reported as small.
Code is available, which may reduce implementation burden.

findings.claim: Quest's accuracy evidence is limited to specific long-context models and benchmarks, with question/instruction decoding simulated token-by-token, so generalization to other architectures and tasks is not fully established.
findings.mechanism: Evaluations use LongChat-v1.5-7b-32k and Yarn-Llama-2-7b-128k on PG19, passkey retrieval, and six LongBench datasets; the question or instruction part is fed token by token to simulate decoding.

evidence.support_description: The paper evaluates two long-context models and the listed datasets.
The paper simulates decoding by feeding the task's question and instruction to the model token by token.

caveats: The paper claims the memory-load reduction is universal across models.
Kernel-level evaluation uses Llama2-7B.

findings.claim: Quest's end-to-end evaluation is for single-batch decode-stage latency; benefits for batched serving, prefill, or other inference stages are not demonstrated.
findings.mechanism: Quest optimizes self-attention memory movement in the decode stage, and the end-to-end experiment measures average latency of generating one token in single-batch scenarios.

evidence.support_description: The framework is deployed into real-world single-batch scenarios, measuring average latency of generating one token in the decode stage.
The decode stage dominates inference time, while prefill happens only once per request.

caveats: Kernel-level speedups may apply more broadly.
The paper focuses on decode-stage latency.

findings.claim: Quest relies on the empirical assumption that only a small portion of KV cache tokens is critical; tasks or layers requiring dense attention can lose important tokens under a small Top-K budget.
findings.mechanism: Quest performs sparse attention only on Top-K selected pages; if critical tokens are numerous or spread across more than K pages, some important tokens are excluded.

evidence.support_description: Apart from the first two layers, less than 10% of tokens are needed for similar accuracy, but the first two layers have low sparsity.
Accuracy depends on the KV cache budget and dataset; Quest with a 1K budget is comparable on evaluated tasks.

caveats: Evaluated tasks show near-lossless accuracy at sufficient budget.
Attention sparsity is empirical and not guaranteed for all workloads.

findings.claim: The paper does not explain why the first two layers have low sparsity or provide an automatic rule for choosing which layers to skip for new models.
findings.mechanism: Layer-wise sparsity is empirically observed and used to justify skipping the first two layers, but the underlying cause and a general layer-selection procedure are not established.
conditions: applying Quest to a different LLM

evidence.support_description: The first two layers have low sparsity, so Quest is applied only on later layers; the paper says skipping the first two layers is orthogonal to the selection algorithm.

caveats: The paper suggests the skip choice is orthogonal to the KV cache selection algorithm.
Layer choice may need empirical profiling for each model.

findings.claim: AWQ's per-channel scaling can increase quantization error for non-salient channels when the group quantization scale grows, so the scaling factor must be balanced and cannot be made arbitrarily large.
findings.mechanism: Scaling salient channels up can change the group's maximum absolute weight and thus the quantization scale Δ; a larger Δ amplifies relative error for non-salient channels in the same group.
conditions: Large scaling factor or many salient channels in a group.
Group quantization scale Δ is determined by the maximum absolute weight.

evidence.support_description: Table 2 shows best perplexity at s=2; larger s increases the percentage of changed Δ and can damage accuracy; text states non-salient-channel error is amplified when Δ increases.

caveats: Paper reports best perplexity at s=2 for OPT-6.7B under INT3-g128.
AWQ searches α to balance protection of salient and non-salient channels.
For s<2, the percentage of changed Δ is reported to be small.

findings.claim: AWQ does not directly optimize the non-differentiable quantization objective; it restricts scaling to a simple activation-magnitude power form and grid-searches one hyperparameter, so the found scales may be suboptimal.
findings.mechanism: Quantization is non-differentiable and approximate gradients were found unstable; AWQ uses s=s_X^α and a grid search over α in [0,1], plus weight clipping.

evidence.support_description: The objective is non-differentiable; authors define the search space s=s_X^α and grid-search α; grid size is 20.

caveats: The simple search is reported to be stable and effective in experiments.
The paper does not claim global optimality of the searched scales.
Weight clipping is also applied to minimize MSE.

findings.claim: The saliency criterion is based on the empirical hypothesis that channels with larger activation magnitudes are more important; this mechanism is not theoretically established and may not hold universally.
findings.mechanism: AWQ identifies salient weight channels by activation distribution rather than weight magnitude, assuming larger input-feature magnitudes correspond to more important features.
conditions: Activation statistics collected from a calibration set.

evidence.support_description: Paper states it hypothesizes larger input features are generally more important; activation-based selection works while weight-based and random selection do not.

caveats: The hypothesis is supported empirically on OPT and LLaMA-family models.
AWQ scales all channels rather than keeping selected channels in FP16.
Activation magnitude is measured per channel.

findings.claim: AWQ still depends on a calibration set, and calibration-set distribution affects quantized accuracy; using a different distribution from evaluation is worse than matching distributions.
findings.mechanism: AWQ computes per-channel average activation magnitudes from calibration data to set scaling factors; distribution shift changes these statistics.
conditions: Calibration data distribution differs from evaluation domain.
INT3-g128 OPT-6.7B in the reported experiment.

evidence.support_description: Same calibration/evaluation distribution works best; cross-distribution increases perplexity by 0.5-0.6 for AWQ, while GPTQ degrades more.

caveats: AWQ is reported to be more robust and data-efficient than GPTQ.
Only a 0.5-0.6 perplexity increase is reported in the cross-distribution test.
Main experiments use a small calibration set from the Pile.

findings.claim: AWQ is weight-only W4A16 quantization; it does not reduce activation or KV-cache precision, and practical speedup requires memory-bound generation plus fused dequantization kernels and platform-specific packing.
findings.mechanism: AWQ reduces weight memory; generation is memory-bound, but W4A16 needs on-the-fly dequantization because hardware lacks INT4×FP16 multiply; TinyChat fuses dequantization and uses SIMD-aware packing.
conditions: TinyChat or equivalent optimized kernels available.
Platform-specific weight packing, e.g., ARM NEON or GPU packing.

evidence.support_description: Generation is memory-bound and weight access dominates; W4A16 dequantization must be fused into the main computation loop; platform-specific packing is used.

caveats: The context stage is less memory-bound and benefits less.
TinyChat reports 3.2-3.3× average speedup over HuggingFace FP16.
AWQ can reduce memory footprint even when speedup is not realized.

findings.claim: At extreme low-bit quantization such as INT2, AWQ is not presented as a standalone solution; the paper combines AWQ with GPTQ to improve performance.
findings.mechanism: INT2 quantization error is severe; AWQ scaling is orthogonal to GPTQ reconstruction and is combined with it under INT2-g64.
conditions: Limited device memory requiring extreme low-bit.
OPT model family in the reported experiment.

evidence.support_description: Table 9 reports AWQ+GPTQ for INT2-g64; text says AWQ is orthogonal to GPTQ and can be combined to improve INT2.

caveats: AWQ alone is not reported in Table 9 for INT2.
RTN fails at INT2.
AWQ+GPTQ still has higher perplexity than FP16.

findings.claim: For multimodal models, AWQ is applied only to the language part; the vision components are not quantized in the reported VLM experiments.
findings.mechanism: The language model dominates model size, so AWQ quantizes language weights while leaving vision encoder and other components in higher precision.
conditions: VLM/LMM quantization, e.g., OpenFlamingo, LLaVA, VILA.
Reported experiments quantize only the language part.

evidence.support_description: Text states: 'We only quantize the language part of the model since it dominates the model size.'

caveats: AWQ shows lossless or improved VLM benchmark results.
This is not full multimodal model compression.
Vision encoder may remain FP16.

findings.claim: AWQ's reported quantization settings are mainly grouped weight-only INT4/INT3 with group size 128; other bit-widths, group sizes, or hardware may require additional tuning or methods.
findings.mechanism: Group size 128 and INT4/INT3 are used throughout; α grid and clipping are tuned for these settings; lower bit or different grouping changes quantization error and scaling behavior.
conditions: Bit precision outside INT4/INT3, e.g., INT2.

evidence.support_description: Paper states group size 128 is used throughout except otherwise specified and focuses on INT4/INT3; INT2 is tested with GPTQ combination.

caveats: Paper also tests Mistral/Mixtral and INT2 with GPTQ.
AWQ is orthogonal to GPTQ.
This is not a claim that other settings fail, only that they are less covered.
